title: The Flag Outside My Window
deck: We inherited a flag, a homeland, and the dream of independence—but seventy-nine years later, have we given every citizen the freedom, dignity, and security that independence was meant to promise? Perhaps the birth of a country was only the beginning of the struggle for freedom.
author: Dur E Najaf 2nd Year MBBS- SMC
body: Every year, on the 14th of August, my street changed its clothes. Green flags appeared on rooftops. Children painted little crescents on their cheeks. Loudspeakers filled the morning with songs about freedom, sacrifice, and a country that had once been dreamed into existence. And every year, I stood by the same window and wondered, What exactly are we celebrating? I was a child when I first asked my father that question. “Independence,” he said, smiling. “Independence from whom?” I asked. He paused. And then said, “From the British.” I looked outside at the flag fluttering above our neighbour's house. “Then we are free?” “Yes.” I believed him. Children are generous with their faith. Years passed… I grew older, and the word independence grew heavier; I watched my mother count notes at the kitchen table before deciding whether we could afford medicine or groceries. I watched my father return home exhausted, his hands carrying the smell of a day's labour and his eyes carrying the weight of tomorrow. I watched a student speak of his rights. The crowd answered with applause. Then came the silence. Not the silence of disagreement. The other kind, the kind that arrives when a microphone is switched off before a truth can travel too far. I watched people look around before speaking about power, as though even words had begun to need permission. I watched ordinary men turn ordinary sentences into calculations; What can I say? Who can hear me? What will happen if I do? … And slowly, painfully, the question I had asked my father as a child found its way back to me, If a nation is free, why are its people still learning how to whisper?? Perhaps independence was never supposed to mean that every morning would be easy. Perhaps a country could be poor and still be free. Perhaps it could stumble, fail, fall, and rise again. But how could we call ourselves completely independent when so many people were still fighting battles that had nothing to do with borders?? A mother fighting to feed her children. A worker fighting to be paid fairly. A student fighting for an education. A citizen fighting simply to be heard. A family praying for peace instead of planning their future. What kind of freedom is it when the first question in a man's mind is not, “What do I want to become?” But, “How will I earn enough to survive?”

On the fourteenth of August, the streets still filled with flags. I loved the sight of them. I still do. Because a flag is not merely cloth. It carries the memory of people who once believed that tomorrow could be different from yesterday. And perhaps that is what hurts the most. We inherited their dream. But did we inherit their freedom? We speak proudly of religious freedom, yet religion existed long before the country did. We celebrate a homeland where Muslims could live according to their faith. But freedom of faith means little if we cannot grant one another the freedom to question, disagree, or think differently without fear. We call ourselves independent, Yet sometimes the loudest chains are the ones nobody can see. Fear. Silence. Poverty. Inequality. Power. Live to survive. That night, I walked through my neighborhood. A little boy was waving a flag from the roof of his house. His father stood behind him. “Pakistan Zindabad!” the boy shouted. His voice was so pure that I stopped walking.

For a moment, I felt ashamed of my questions. Then I looked at him more carefully. He was barefoot. His shirt was faded. The light above his house flickered.
And suddenly I understood something.
Perhaps the boy was not wrong.
Perhaps neither was I.

He was celebrating the Pakistan we were promised. I was mourning the Pakistan we had failed to become. The difference mattered. Because loving a country does not mean pretending it has no wounds. Sometimes love means refusing to call a wound a birthmark. Sometimes patriotism is not the loudest voice in the crowd. Sometimes patriotism is the person who asks an uncomfortable question because they still believe the country can become better. So, I looked at the flag again. It moved gently in the night wind. And I thought of 1947. Of people leaving homes they had known all their lives. Of trains carrying dreams, grief, fear, and hope. Of people who believed that the next generation would inherit something greater than themselves. They did not sacrifice so that we could merely change the name of our rulers. They dreamed of dignity. Of justice. Of safety. Of equality. Of a place where a person could live without fear. Maybe independence was never meant to end on the day a new flag was raised. Maybe that was only the beginning. Because a nation can win its freedom from a foreign ruler and still spend decades trying to free its people from hunger, fear, injustice, inequality, ignorance, and silence. And perhaps that is the independence we are still waiting for. Not independence from another country. But independence from everything that prevents a human being from living as a human being. The next morning, the flags were still everywhere. Some were torn. Some were hanging crookedly. Some had fallen into the streets. Children were still singing. People were still buying breakfast. Buses were still honking. Life was still happening. I stood beside my window. And for the first time, I did not ask, “Are we independent?” I asked something harder. “What will we do with the independence we were given?” … Because, perhaps we have been celebrating the birth of a country for seventy-nine years, But freedom? Freedom may still be waiting for its birthday…
